name: Jorge Berríos
location: Clermont, Florida (54 years in Puerto Rico before that)
tagline: Retired physician, collector of more than 200 radios, and the creator behind more than 50 Facebook shortwave groups.
quote: Radio means everything to me. I like to hear the world news, different cultures and customs of different countries.
radio: More than 200 radios. Favorites include the Sony ICF-2010, Panasonic RF-2200, Zenith Royal 3000-1 Trans-Oceanic and Grundig Satellit 800 Millennium, plus the MLite-880 SDR
antenna: Mostly the radio's built-in telescopic whip, with a magnetic loop antenna on occasion
since: Since his teens; seriously for about 12 years

gallery.alt: Shelves of portable and emergency radios from Jorge Berríos's collection
Jorge Berríos's radio room, including a Grundig Satellit 800 Millennium

story.p: Jorge lived in Puerto Rico for 54 years. A doctor specializing in Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, he practiced for 20 years at the VA Medical Center in San Juan and several more at the UDH Puerto Rico Medical Center, before retiring due to a disability in 2012. That same year he moved to Clermont, Florida, where he lives with his wife of 42 years, Tere Pizarro.

Jorge started listening as a teenager, across shortwave, medium wave, FM and the NOAA weather band. He got seriously into shortwave listening about 12 years ago, after retiring, and the hobby has grown ever since. These days he also listens to airband traffic from Orlando's airport.
His most memorable DX catch, and the QSL that came with it, was Radio Exterior de España, Spain's international shortwave service.

Jorge is the creator and administrator of more than 50 Facebook shortwave radio groups. His largest include Shortwave Radio Listeners Club, a public group with about 42,000 members, and DX Shortwave Radio Listener, with about 40,000 (member counts as of October 2026). Together they make him one of the busiest community builders in the hobby.

His collection runs from classics like the Zenith Trans-Oceanic and Sony ICF-2010 to the latest SDRs. He enjoys the MLite-880 SDR and says he enjoys using the latest technology as much as the vintage sets.

ask: What was your most memorable QSL card? Share it on our Radio Memories page.

name: Matt Brown
tagline: 55 years of listening, from a Patrolman 9 and Radio Nederland QSL cards to monthly DX reports on the air.
quote: My brother happened to get a radio that had shortwave capability, redefining for my young self what distant listening really was.

stats.l: SWLs in his RFI listeners club

radio: Sangean 803, Panasonic RF-2200 and XHDATA D-219 are his primary radios
antenna: A long wire for now, with a better loop antenna planned for when he returns to more serious listening

story.p: Matt fell in love with distant listening around age 8, tuning far-off AM stations. In the 1960s there was much less noise on the AM band, so stations from around the U.S. came in easily, and he loved the idea of hearing them.

At 11 or 12 his brother got a radio with shortwave, which redefined what distant listening meant. His dad bought him a Patrolman 9, and his very first QSL cards followed: Radio Nederland in Holland, then Radio Moscow, HCJB and more.

story.h: The night Idi Amin came on the air
story.p: His most memorable shortwave moment: Radio Uganda could be received only sporadically back then, but one evening he tuned in and listened to the dictator Idi Amin ramble on endlessly with his political diatribes against the world. Because it was Idi Amin himself, it made for a very memorable experience.

list: Taped monthly DX reports that were broadcast on Adventist World Radio India, Radio Clarín in Santo Domingo, and Austrian Radio
Headed a group of some 25 SWLs of Radio France Internationale and published a monthly “Listeners Club” bulletin for almost two years
Wrote a few simple articles about the hobby for the old SPEEDX shortwave listeners club’s monthly bulletin

story.p: Matt has been a more casual listener for the last 10 to 15 years, but the dial still calls. His long wire antenna gets him by for now, and a better loop is on the list for the day he gets back to more serious listening.
He has “so much more to write about” and has thought about writing an academic-style paper for people curious about shortwave in its golden era, the 1970s and 1980s. “We’ll see,” he says.

ask: Did you hear Radio Uganda, or another golden-era broadcast you still remember? Share it on our Radio Memories page.

name: Raul Alfonso Guerrero
location: Born in Cartagena, Colombia — now in Canada
radio: 500+ radios over a lifetime — nearly 100 still in active collection, all working and looking like new
antenna: Indoor and outdoor configurations — reviews and tests both
favorite_freq: Voice of Free China (Radio Taiwan International) — where the true passion began
why: At age four I picked up my father's transistor radio and accidentally switched it to SW. Turning the dial, I heard voices in completely unfamiliar languages and grasped that the signal was coming from far away. My brother and I each received a radio the following Christmas — single band MW models made in Hong Kong. It was exciting to pick up stations from the Caribbean islands and Florida at night. The true passion began one night while using a four-band radio cassette player — I heard a female voice, Maria Francisca, broadcasting for The Voice of Free China, known today as Radio Taiwan International. During the program they read the mailing address on air. The next day I sent a letter. Two months later I received a large envelope filled with magazines, stickers, pennants, and my first QSL card. I had no idea stations replied to mail. It was a wonderful surprise. Using some savings I bought my first dedicated shortwave radio — a National RF-9L, the smallest on the market at the time. It was the Cold War era, the golden age of shortwave, when the conflict was fought not with bombs but with the ideological propaganda of each side. I wrote to every station I could pick up and they all replied with QSL cards and souvenirs. There were also contests with fabulous prizes — ranging from shortwave radios to trips to the station's home country.
best_catch: More than 500 radios have passed through my hands since that first National RF-9L. I still keep nearly 100 of them — all working and looking like new. Today I share my experience with radio listeners around the world through Facebook groups, WhatsApp groups, and my YouTube channel, where I review new radios, cover innovations, and post real-world reception tests. Radio faces threats from new technologies and the cost of keeping stations on the air — but I firmly believe radio is here to stay. It has done so much good for humanity and in my own case has transported me to new cultures, languages, and knowledge. Long live radio!
